title: Partner API Stalled? How Vertical SaaS Ships AI Features Anyway
summary: The partner program says six months minimum. Run two tracks: apply in week 1 and build on a design partner's own account through Integuru, so your first cohort is live in weeks 3 to 4. A week-by-week plan, and when to wait instead.
body_markdown:
Your AI ordering assistant is demo-ready. The restaurants that have been testing it for weeks want it live this quarter. Then the partner program for the POS platform they run replies: six months minimum, then certification.


You do not have to choose between waiting and giving up on the platform. Run two tracks: submit the partner application in week 1, and build the same integration through Integuru on a design partner's own account, so a first cohort of customers is live in weeks 3 and 4. If the official API later covers your workflow, you migrate to it. If it never does, you have already shipped.


At Integuru, we build integrations for vertical SaaS platforms in exactly this position, across restaurant POS, field service and proptech, and the pattern repeats. This post covers what the wait costs, why the queues run long, the week-by-week plan, what to tell customers and counsel, and the cases where you should wait instead.


### **What does a six-month wait actually cost?**


A six-month wait costs a platform in this position three things: design-partner momentum, competitive ground, and the write access its AI feature needs. None of them show up on a roadmap slide.


-


**Design partners cool off.** They agreed to test because the assistant solved a problem this quarter. Six months of "almost live" turns an enthusiastic design partner into a polite one, and your feedback loop stops with them.


-


**Competitors ship.** A competitor that reaches the same platform by any route will be in your prospects' demos while you sit in a review queue, and a working order in a demo beats a roadmap promise.


-


**The feature launches read-only.** Partner programs often hold back write endpoints, and for an ordering assistant that is the whole job. An assistant that can read a menu but cannot place or change an order is a dashboard with a chat box.


The same shape shows up outside restaurants. A field service scheduler that can see jobs but cannot create them. A proptech assistant that can read a lease but cannot post a work order. The AI feature is ready, and the access it depends on is the part stuck in a queue.


### **Why do partner program queues run so long?**


Partner program queues run long because the platform is reviewing more than your code. Programs commonly bundle a security and certification review, a commercial agreement that may include revenue share or per-call fees, and a decision about which endpoints to expose, and write endpoints are the ones most often left out. None of that is unreasonable, but none of it runs on your launch calendar.


A platform that holds data for many businesses has good reasons to be slow about who touches it, and you would want the same caution from the platform your own customers trust. What the queue length cannot tell you is whether the finished API will cover your workflow, and that is the thing you are really waiting to learn. So use week 1 to find out early: ask which endpoints the program covers, whether writes are included, and what certification and commercial terms apply. Even a partial reply is something you can plan around.


### **What is the dual-track plan, week by week?**


Dual track means applying to the platform's partner program and building the integration through Integuru in the same weeks. In week 1 you apply and scope. In weeks 1 to 2 a sandbox integration is built on a design partner's own account. In weeks 3 to 4 the first cohort goes to production. From month 6, you check whether the official API covers the workflow and migrate where it does.

Take the ordering assistant as an illustrative scope, not a quote: read the menu and item availability, create an order, and mark an item unavailable. Three actions, two of them writes. That is enough to demo, enough to put in front of a first cohort, and small enough that a sandbox build fits inside a sprint.


Two details matter more than the calendar.


**Write one scope and use it twice.** The workflow description you draft for the partner application is the same document Integuru scopes the build from. Writing it once keeps the two tracks from drifting apart, and it makes the month-6 comparison trivial because both sides were measured against the same list of actions.


**Put the integration behind your own adapter.** Treat the Integuru endpoint as an ordinary HTTP call, wrapped in one function with a timeout, a typed error and a latency log line. When the official API arrives, you swap the implementation behind that function one action at a time instead of rewriting the feature. The[one-sprint POC guide](https://www.integuru.com/blog/integration-poc-one-sprint) walks through that adapter in detail.


**Running the Integuru track.** There are two ways to do it. A developer on your team can use the CLI:` integuru platform create` returns a link where the design partner enters their own platform login in the browser, and` integuru integration create` starts a builder run that takes roughly 10 to 20 minutes for a draft. The Free plan ($0, 1 platform, 1 account, 100 API calls a month) is enough to prove the path on one account but not to carry a cohort, and it does not include the 24/7 maintenance.


For the cohort, the Production plan starts at $499 a month for one platform and one account with 10,000 API calls, 24/7 on-call maintenance and authentication auto-healing, with additional accounts from $150 a month each for the first ten (prices as of November 2026). If you would rather not own the build at all, the[Fully Managed Service](https://www.integuru.com/managed-service) builds each requested integration to a sandbox with no separate build fee, typically in a few days, and runs it with 24/7 on-call maintenance on custom pricing.


The maintenance is what makes the six months livable. When the platform changes its login flow or session handling, Integuru's on-call team repairs the integration, so your engineers spend the wait shipping product instead of patching access. If your customer contracts need a contractual uptime commitment, ask about an SLA on the Fully Managed Service. The 99.9%+ figure on the site is a measured success rate, not a contract.


### **What do you tell customers and legal?**


Tell customers and counsel the same plain thing: every connection runs on the customer's own account, with the customer's own credentials, on a platform that requires a login. Integuru does not scrape public pages, create fake accounts, or reuse one customer's credentials for another. The design partner agrees in writing and enters their own login themselves.


Then say the uncomfortable part out loud, because your counsel will. A platform's Terms of Service governs its account holders whether a person clicks through a browser or an authenticated request does the same action, and some terms address automated access or sharing credentials with a service provider. Using Integuru does not create a violation where none existed. It also does not erase a restriction a platform has written into its terms. Before any code is written, Integuru's team reads the target platform's policy as part of scoping, and a hard blocker is raised then, before engineering time is spent. The[trust page](https://www.integuru.com/trust) sets out that review, and the[plain-language legal guide](https://www.integuru.com/blog/reverse-engineering-private-api-legal) covers the three separate legal questions people usually mean. Neither replaces your own counsel. Decide with them what you tell the platform's partner team, and do not misdescribe how the integration works in your application.


When a restaurant owner asks what exactly you are connecting to,[user-permissioned access](https://www.integuru.com/blog/user-permissioned-api-access) is the answer to give: their account, their credentials, their consent, and no view of anyone else's data.


### **When should you wait instead?**


Wait when the official API covers the workflow and the timeline fits. If the partner team answers in week 1 that every action in your scope is covered, writes included, and the launch date sits after the approval date, the official route is simpler to explain, simpler to own and sanctioned by the platform. Integuru's scoping process starts from the same place: we check for an official API or partner program first, and we recommend it whenever it covers the workflow.


Two other cases change the plan. If scoping finds a hard blocker in the platform's terms, such as an explicit prohibition we cannot honor, we tell you before building anything, and the right move is to stay in the partner queue or negotiate. And if what you want from the partner program includes the marketplace listing and co-selling channel that often comes with it, a generated integration does not replace that, which is a reason to keep the application alive even after you have shipped.


At month 6, run the comparison action by action:


-


**Coverage:** does the official API do every action in your scope, including the writes?


-


**Terms:** what do certification, revenue share or per-call fees cost against what you pay now?


-


**Limits:** do the rate limits and account volumes fit the cohort you have grown?


-


**Channel:** does the listing add customers you would not otherwise reach?


Migrate the actions where the official API wins, and keep the rest on the integration that already works. The[guide to connecting software without an API](https://www.integuru.com/blog/how-to-connect-software-without-apis) compares the other routes if you want the full option set.


### **FAQ**


**Can we run a partner application and an Integuru integration at the same time?**


Yes. Integuru recommends running them in parallel and recommends the official route when it covers your workflow. The partner application proceeds on its own timeline while Integuru builds a sandbox integration on a design partner's own account. Your platform's terms and your counsel still decide what you disclose to the partner team.


**How long does it take to get a first cohort live without waiting for partner approval?**


On the plan above, a sandbox build takes days and the first cohort reaches production in weeks 3 and 4. Integuru's managed service typically delivers a requested integration in a few days, and a CLI builder run produces a draft in roughly 10 to 20 minutes. Your own wiring, testing and cohort consent set the rest of the calendar.


**Is it allowed to connect customers' accounts while a partner application is pending?**


It depends on the platform's terms, which is why scoping reads them first. Integuru integrations run only on authenticated accounts, with the customer's own credentials and consent, but a platform's Terms of Service can still restrict automated access. Integuru flags hard blockers before building. Take the specifics to your own counsel.
